title: Understanding Cold Starts in LLM Inference
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: Understanding Cold Starts in LLM Inference
In the last few articles, I have been thinking about autoscaling, routing, KV cache, and distributed inference.
Autoscaling sounds straightforward:

Traffic increases
↓
Add another replica
↓
More capacity
But there is an important gap hidden inside this picture.

We decided that we need
another inference replica.

How long before that replica
can actually generate tokens?
That gap is the cold start.
And with LLM inference, starting a replica can mean much more than simply starting a container.
What exactly is a cold start?
A cold start is the work required to turn inactive capacity into a model that is actually ready to serve inference requests.
For an LLM server, that can look roughly like this:

Get a machine
↓
Start the container
↓
Start the inference runtime
↓
Find and load the model weights
↓
Move the weights onto the GPU
↓
Prepare GPU memory and execution
↓
Warm up the engine
↓
Start serving requests
I had seen diagrams like this before.
But terms such as initialize runtime or load model weights do not explain much by themselves.
So what is actually happening?
What does “get infrastructure” mean?
Suppose Kubernetes decides that another model-server pod is required.
If an existing node has enough free GPU capacity, Kubernetes can schedule the pod there.
But imagine every GPU is already occupied.
Now the new pod remains pending.
The cluster autoscaler may then ask the cloud provider for another GPU machine.
That means the cloud has to do things such as:

allocate the VM or bare-metal machine
↓
boot the operating system
↓
initialize networking
↓
attach required storage
↓
start Kubernetes components
↓
register the node with the cluster
Only after that can Kubernetes place the model-server pod on it.
So sometimes the biggest cold start has nothing to do with the model yet.
The machine itself did not exist.
What happens during a container cold start?
Now assume the machine exists.
Kubernetes wants to start something like a vLLM model-server container.
First it needs the container image.
If the image is already cached on that node, this can be relatively quick.
But if it is not cached:

Container Registry
↓
download image layers
↓
unpack them onto the node
↓
create the container
↓
start the inference process
A large inference image may contain Python, CUDA libraries, PyTorch, the inference engine, and many other dependencies.
So downloading and unpacking the image itself can take time.
This is why:
Pod created
does not mean:
Model ready
The application has only started its journey.
What does “initialize the runtime” actually mean?
Now the inference program starts.
For example, imagine we started vLLM.
Before it can generate anything, the program has to understand the environment it is running in.
It may need to:

Read the model configuration.
Load the tokenizer configuration.
Detect available GPUs.
Initialize CUDA.
Decide how the model will be split if multiple GPUs are used.
Create communication between GPU workers.
Work out how much memory can be used for KV cache.
Create internal schedulers and memory managers.
So when I say:
initialize inference runtime
I really mean:

Build all the machinery
that will run the model.
The weights are only one part of that machinery.
Why does CUDA initialization take time?
The GPU is physically present, but our process cannot simply start sending matrix multiplications to it.
The CUDA runtime first needs to establish the application's connection to the GPU.
Conceptually:

Inference process
↓
CUDA runtime / driver
↓
GPU
The process needs GPU contexts, memory management structures, streams, and other runtime resources.
If we are using several GPUs, the engine also has to make those workers aware of each other.
For tensor parallel inference, for example:
GPU 0 ←→ GPU 1 ←→ GPU 2 ←→ GPU 3
Parts of every layer may be distributed across those GPUs.
They therefore need communication channels before inference can work correctly.
This is one reason a distributed replica has more startup work than a simple single-GPU process.
What does “load the model weights” mean?
This was one phrase I wanted to understand more clearly.
A model is ultimately stored as files somewhere.
For example:

Model repository
Object Storage
Network filesystem
Local SSD
Those files contain billions of learned parameter values.
When we start the inference server, those parameters must become available to the inference process.
There are two very different situations.
The model is already stored locally
Then there may be no internet or object-storage download at all.
The engine reads the model files from local disk.

Local SSD
↓
Inference process
The model is not available locally
Now it may first need to come across the network.

Model repository / Object Storage
↓
Network
↓
Node storage or memory
So when someone says:
Model loading took 60 seconds.
I now want to ask:

Was the model already local?

Or did we spend most of that
time downloading it?
Those are very different problems.
What does “read model files” mean?
Suppose the model is already on an NVMe disk.
The model might still be tens or hundreds of gigabytes.
The storage device has to read all those bytes.
Very roughly:

100 GB model

Storage reads at 2 GB/s

Even perfect sequential reading
would take about 50 seconds.
Real systems are more complicated, but the intuition is useful.
Large-model startup is partly a data movement problem.
The GPU can be incredibly fast at matrix multiplication and still sit waiting for the model to arrive.
What does “deserialize the weights” mean?
The model file is just stored data.
Something like:
model.safetensors
contains parameter values plus information describing what those values represent.
The runtime needs to turn that stored representation into tensors that the model code can use.
Conceptually:

Bytes inside model file

↓ interpret them as

Tensor:
shape = 4096 × 4096
dtype = FP16
belongs to layer 12
That conversion from stored model representation into usable tensor structures is what people mean by deserialization.
It is not the model “learning” anything.
We are simply rebuilding the model from its saved representation.
What does “allocate memory” mean?
Before putting model weights onto a GPU, the runtime needs space to put them.
Imagine the GPU has:
80 GB HBM
The inference engine has to divide that memory among things such as:

Model weights
KV cache
Temporary computation buffers
Runtime overhead
So the engine reserves memory for these different purposes.
For example:

80 GB GPU

50 GB → model
24 GB → KV cache
6 GB  → runtime/workspace
The actual numbers vary significantly, but this is the idea.
This is another reason model startup is not simply:
copy file → GPU
The engine first has to construct the memory environment in which inference will happen.
What does “copy the weights to the GPU” mean?
Eventually those parameter values need to be accessible by the GPU.
A simplified path might be:

SSD
↓
CPU memory
↓
PCIe
↓
GPU HBM
Different runtimes can optimize this path, so it is not always exactly this sequence.
But something fundamental remains true:

Large amounts of data
have to move.
If 100 GB of weights need to cross a connection, the bandwidth of that connection matters.
This is why cold-start performance can depend on:

storage speed
network speed
PCIe bandwidth
model size
number of GPUs
model format
not simply GPU FLOPS.
What does “initialize tensors” mean?
Once the weight data is available, the framework has to associate it with the correct parts of the neural network.
For example:

Layer 0 attention weights
Layer 0 MLP weights

Layer 1 attention weights
Layer 1 MLP weights

...
If tensor parallelism is being used, the runtime may also need to determine which GPU owns which portion.
For example:

Weight matrix

GPU 0 → shard 1
GPU 1 → shard 2
GPU 2 → shard 3
GPU 3 → shard 4
The model is effectively being reconstructed in the form required for execution.
What does “prepare the inference engine” mean?
Now we have the model.
But the engine still needs infrastructure around it.
Take vLLM as an example.
It needs things such as:

Scheduler
KV Cache Manager
GPU Workers
Model Executor
PagedAttention structures
The scheduler needs to know how requests will be batched.
The KV Cache Manager needs memory blocks it can assign to requests.
GPU workers need to be initialized.
The model executor needs to know how computation will be launched.
So:
Weights loaded
still does not necessarily mean:
Inference engine completely ready
Why does the engine sometimes run a warm-up?
Suppose everything is loaded.
The engine may still execute one or more test requests before declaring itself fully ready.
Why?
Because the first execution may trigger additional setup.
Depending on the runtime, this can include things such as:

loading or compiling GPU kernels
building execution paths
capturing CUDA graphs
creating temporary buffers
testing memory usage
Think of it almost like starting a car.
The engine exists.
The fuel is there.
But we still start the engine before driving onto the highway.
A warm-up request lets the system exercise the important inference path before a real user does.
So where does cold-start time actually go?
Now the picture is much easier for me to understand.

Need capacity
↓
Maybe create a machine
        infrastructure time

↓
Maybe download the container
        image/network time

↓
Start inference application
        process/runtime time

↓
Maybe download model
        network/storage time

↓
Read model files
        storage time

↓
Build tensors and model structure
        CPU/runtime work

↓
Move model onto GPUs
        memory-transfer time

↓
Initialize GPU workers
        CUDA/distributed setup

↓
Reserve KV cache and workspaces
        memory setup

↓
Warm up execution
        kernels/graphs/runtime work

↓
Ready
Now “cold start” no longer feels like one mysterious number.
It is the sum of several different startup costs.
Is a cold KV cache the same thing?
No, and I think this distinction is especially important.
Suppose the server has finished everything above.
The model is loaded.
The engine is ready.
It can serve traffic.
But imagine a request arrives with a large system prompt the replica has never processed.
The model is warm.
The prefix cache is cold.
So the complete prefill still needs to happen.

Model warm
+
Prefix cache cold
Later, if another request uses the same reusable prefix:

Model warm
+
Prefix cache warm
The server may avoid repeating some of that prefill work.
So I now separate these two ideas:

Model cold start
=
How long until I can serve?

Cache coldness
=
How much useful inference state
have I already built?
What happens when autoscaling adds a new replica?
This connects cold starts directly with my previous articles on KV-cache-aware routing.
Imagine:

Replica A
Replica B
have been serving traffic for an hour.
They may already contain useful prefix-cache state.
Traffic increases.
Autoscaling creates:
Replica C
Replica C first pays its startup cost.
Then it becomes Ready.
But Replica C may still have almost no useful cached prefixes.
Now a request arrives.
Replica A might have:

longer queue
+
useful prefix already cached
Replica C might have:

empty queue
+
cold prefix cache
Which one should the router choose?
Now routing is no longer simply:

Send traffic to
the least busy replica.
The router may be balancing:

queue depth
+
cache locality
+
available memory
+
replica readiness
That is why inference-aware routing becomes so interesting.
How does this become even harder with model routing?
Now imagine the router is not just choosing between replicas of the same model.
It can choose between completely different models.
For example:

Small Model
→ already running

Large Model
→ currently scaled to zero
A complex request arrives.
Maybe the large model would produce the better result.
But choosing it could mean:

Start infrastructure
↓
Start container
↓
Load large model
↓
Initialize GPUs
↓
Warm engine
↓
Finally run request
So the routing decision is no longer only:
Which model is best?
It can become:

Which model is good enough?

Which model is already warm?

How much will starting another
model delay this request?

Is that extra quality
worth the startup latency?
And there is another issue.
Suppose a conversation started on Model A.
Then halfway through we route it to Model B.
Even if Model B is already running, Model B does not magically inherit Model A's KV cache.
It will usually need to process the conversation context itself.
So switching models can introduce another cost:

Model routing
↓
Different model
↓
Existing KV state cannot simply be reused
↓
Context needs prefill again
This makes model routing very different from ordinary HTTP load balancing.
A request carries useful computational history with it.
Why does this matter so much for autoscaling?
Because the autoscaler can make the correct decision and users can still experience poor latency.
For example:

10:00:00
Traffic spike begins

10:00:10
Autoscaler detects it

10:00:15
New replica requested

10:01:30
Replica finally becomes ready
The autoscaler worked.
But there was still more than a minute during which demand exceeded available serving capacity.
That leads to the metric I find most useful here:
Time to Usable Capacity
Not:

How quickly did Kubernetes
create a pod?
But:

How long after deciding
that I need more capacity

did I actually get a model
capable of generating tokens?
What is the key intuition?
Cold start is really about turning:
Potential capacity
into:
Usable inference capacity
And that requires much more than simply starting a process.

Infrastructure
↓
Software
↓
Model weights
↓
GPU memory
↓
Inference runtime
↓
Ready
Then, even after the model is Ready:
Cache state builds over time.
That gives me two different warm-up problems to think about:

Can this replica serve?

and

Can this replica serve efficiently
using the state it has already built?
Both matter for autoscaling and routing.
What comes next?
Understanding the cold-start path immediately creates the next question:

Which of these steps
can we eliminate,
hide,
or make faster?
For example:

Do we keep GPU nodes warm?

Do we pre-pull container images?

Can model weights already be
cached on local NVMe?

Should we keep minimum replicas?

Can models be loaded before
traffic arrives?

Can scaling be predictive
instead of reactive?

Can we stream weights differently?

Can warm pools help?

Should small and large models
use different scaling strategies?
So that is where I want to go next:
How Do We Reduce Cold Starts in LLM Inference?
Not just a list of optimizations, but understanding which part of the cold-start path each technique actually removes — and what we pay for it.
